_comment: Storyboard for the Grade 3 Mathematics unit lecture film, Measure It. Rendered by tools/create-ehel-unit-lecture.js. See lecture-video/BRIEF.md. Every beat is one narration clip; art.at names the phrases a picture waits for, and the page refuses to load if a phrase is not in its beat's say. The chapters follow the lesson's own order (steps 4 to 10 of measure-it.html): centimetres, metres and kilometres; grams and kilograms; millilitres and litres; reading a scale; measuring from a mark that is not zero; right angles and turns. Every number said is read off the scale drawn beside it: the pencil spans 0 to 15 and then 2 to 9 on a real ruler, the jugs fill to the 1000, 300 and 500 marks, the balance carries 1000 g against 1 kg, and the pointer sits on the 350 mark of a line printed in hundreds.
title: Measure It
subtitle: Grade 3 Mathematics
objectives: Estimate and measure lengths in centimetres (cm), metres (m) and kilometres (km). Understand the relationship between units.
Estimate and measure the mass of objects in grams (g) and kilograms (kg). Understand the relationship between units.
Estimate and measure capacity in millilitres (ml) and litres (l), and understand their relationships.
Compare angles with a right angle. Recognise that a straight line is equivalent to two right angles or a half turn.
Use instruments that measure length, mass, capacity and temperature.

beats.say: How long is it? How heavy is it? How much does it hold?
Each question has its own tool, its own units and its own scale.
Length is how far it is from one end to the other.

at.ends: from one end to the other

beats.say: A ruler measures it. This pencil runs from zero to fifteen.
So the pencil is fifteen centimetres long.
A hundred centimetres make one metre. A thousand metres make one kilometre.
A door is about two metres. The next town is five kilometres away.
Mass is how heavy a thing is. You weigh it on a scale.
A thousand grams balance one kilogram exactly.
An apple is about a hundred grams. A bag of rice is two kilograms.
Big does not mean heavy. A bag of feathers can weigh less than a stone.
Capacity is how much a container holds.
A thousand millilitres fill one litre.
A teaspoon holds about five millilitres. A mug of tea holds three hundred.
So half a litre is five hundred millilitres, not fifty.
A scale is the marked line on an instrument. What is this pointer reading?
Work out what one small mark is worth first.
Three hundred and four hundred are printed, a hundred apart.
Count the gaps between them, not the marks. There are two.
A hundred shared between two gaps is fifty. The pointer reads three hundred and fifty.

at.share: shared between two gaps is fifty

beats.say: A ruler does not have to start at zero.
This pencil begins at the two and ends at the nine.
Read only the end and you get nine. That is too long.
Count on from the two, not the zero.
Count on, one centimetre at a time: seven centimetres long.

at.count: Count on, one centimetre at a time

beats.say: A right angle is a square corner. It is a quarter turn.
The corner of a book is one. Hold it against any angle to check.
This angle opens less, so it is smaller than a right angle.
This one opens wider, so it is bigger. Long arms do not make a bigger angle.
Two right angles side by side make a straight line, a half turn.
Length in centimetres, mass in grams, capacity in millilitres.
Work out what one mark is worth before you read any scale.
Count on from the start when a ruler starts past zero.
A right angle is a quarter turn, and two of them make a straight line.
